content.p: In the early hours of 9 August 2024, a postgraduate trainee doctor on duty at RG Kar Medical College and Hospital in Kolkata was raped and killed inside a seminar room of the hospital. The court reports used here do not name the victim, and she is referred to here only as the trainee doctor. She was 31 years old and had begun a 36-hour duty shift the day before.

The crime set off protests by doctors and medical students across India and mass night-time marches in cities. On 18 January 2025 a Kolkata court convicted a civic police volunteer, Sanjay Roy, and two days later sentenced him to life imprisonment until the end of his natural life. The CBI, the prosecuting agency, had asked the trial court for the death penalty and the judge declined it. Both the CBI and the West Bengal government then appealed to the Calcutta High Court seeking it, and the court admitted the CBI's appeal. Her parents and many doctors say others were involved; Roy was the only person against whom the CBI had filed a charge sheet when the verdict was given.

The SCC Times report on the judgment records that the trainee doctor started her duty on 8 August. The next day her father was told that she was unwell, and when he reached the hospital he learned she had been raped and killed in the seminar room on the third floor of the chest department. A complaint was lodged under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, India's criminal code. The court later held that she was last seen alive at 2:50 a.m. and that she died between about 4:45 and 5:15 a.m.

Roy, who had worked as a civic volunteer for the Kolkata Police since 2018, was attached to the force's Central Welfare Board and visited the hospital to look after police personnel and their families. Kolkata Police arrested him the day after the body was found.
content.h2: A case taken from the state police
content.p: On 13 August the Calcutta High Court transferred the inquiry to the Central Bureau of Investigation, criticising the local police's handling of it. The Supreme Court also stepped in on its own initiative, Onmanorama reported, to set guidelines on safety for doctors at work and to oversee the investigation.

The question of the first days of the inquiry stayed alive. The CBI arrested Sandip Ghosh, the former principal of the hospital, on 2 September on charges of financial irregularities. On 14 September it arrested him again, together with Abhijit Mondal, the officer in charge of Tala police station, for allegedly tampering with evidence and delaying the filing of a first information report, The Hindu reported. Both are accused and have not been convicted of any offence connected with the killing. Onmanorama reported that because the CBI did not file a charge sheet against them in time, they were granted bail. ABC reported that Ghosh stayed in detention in the separate financial case.
The CBI filed its charge sheet against Roy alone on 7 October 2024, and the court framed the charge on 4 November, according to PTI.

The prosecution relied on forensic evidence, including DNA and toxicology reports, and on CCTV footage that put Roy in the building. Business Standard reported that the CBI's investigation reviewed testimony from more than 120 witnesses. The court held that CCTV, the location of his phone and his own admission under the code of criminal procedure placed him at the scene around the time of the crime. It noted that in the footage he entered the floor with earphones around his neck and left without them, that earphones were found near the body, and that he could not explain why they showed continuous pairing with his phone. It also found a full DNA profile matching Roy in swabs from the victim's body, and her blood on his clothes and footwear.

Roy said he had been framed. His side contended that the earphones were not his, and also that he had gone to a male ward, rested and forgotten them there; the judge said it was hard to believe an outsider could enter and rest in that ward unobserved. The court also rejected his explanation that he was in the area for the surgery of another civic volunteer, because he gave no name or witness. Judge Anirban Das found no evidence of gang rape. On motive, the court held that Roy had drunk alcohol and attacked her on impulse, and was not aware beforehand that she was in the room.

The Sealdah court found Roy guilty on 18 January 2025 and sentenced him two days later. Das gave him rigorous life imprisonment and, under section 66, imprisonment for the rest of his natural life, with the sentences to run together, and fined him 50,000 rupees. He rejected the CBI's request for the death penalty: "I do not consider it as a rarest-of-rare crime," he said, according to ABC. The state was ordered to pay 17 lakh rupees to the victim's family. Local media reported that her father refused it, and that the judge told him the state was responsible for protecting a doctor on duty.

The trainee doctor's parents said they were not satisfied with the investigation and believed others were involved. Their lawyer told Reuters that they had asked for the death penalty and for the people behind what they called a "larger conspiracy" to be brought to justice. After reports that the CBI planned to appeal for the death penalty, her father told PTI that he respected the trial judge's decision and wanted the CBI to find everyone involved.

West Bengal's chief minister, Mamata Banerjee, said she was not satisfied: "From day 1, all of us had demanded death sentence", she said, and she claimed that had the Kolkata Police kept the inquiry it would have secured one. Doctors marched outside the court. One of them told ABC the outcome was "half justice". Sukanta Majumdar, a Union minister, welcomed the conviction but alleged that evidence had been tampered with in the first five days of police inquiry. The politician Brinda Karat asked who was shielding Roy, saying "Roy may be guilty".
content.h2: Appeals and the question of others
content.p: Both the CBI and the West Bengal government appealed to the High Court, seeking capital punishment for Roy. On 7 February 2025 a division bench of Justices Debangsu Basak and Md Sabbar Rashidi dismissed the state's appeal and admitted the CBI's. It reasoned that the CBI had investigated the case and was the prosecuting agency. The bench had reserved its order on 27 January.

The parents petitioned the High Court in December 2024 for a fresh investigation, saying Roy alone could not have committed the crime. On 28 March 2025 the CBI told the court, in a hearing on that petition, that its investigation and a board of medical experts led it to conclude that the incident was not a gang rape, and it said it would continue investigating conspiracy, a cover-up and destruction of evidence. The president of the West Bengal Doctors' Forum, Kaushik Chaki, also told PTI that the CBI must investigate institutional corruption and evidence tampering. No final ruling on the death-penalty appeal had been reported in the latest coverage.

For weeks after the crime, doctors and medical students across India held protests and rallies for justice and for better security for medical staff. The Tribune reported that on 14 August 2024, the eve of Independence Day, tens of thousands of women walked through Kolkata and other cities in the "Reclaim the Night" march. The Tribune said the case also raised concern about violence against health workers.
